segments.narration: Four hundred people once danced continuously until they dropped dead. In 1518, a woman stepped into a French street and started moving uncontrollably.
Within weeks, hundreds joined her. They couldn't stop, weeping in pain as their bloody feet kept stomping.
Authorities even brought in musicians to help, but it only made the obsession deadlier. What was possessing them?
Modern historians finally solved it: severe famine triggered mass psychogenic illness. Extreme psychological stress forced their nervous systems into involuntary spasms.
This outbreak proved human minds under terror can physically drive bodies to death.

verdicts.claim: In July 1518, a woman in Strasbourg began dancing uncontrollably in the street.
verdicts.note: The article confirms that in July 1518, a woman (Frau Troffea) began dancing fervently and uncontrollably in a street in Strasbourg.

verdicts.claim: Around four hundred people eventually joined the outbreak over several weeks.
verdicts.note: The article states that between 50 and 400 people took to dancing over several weeks by August.

verdicts.claim: City officials hired musicians and built stages thinking more dancing would cure the afflicted.
verdicts.note: The article states physicians prescribed the afflicted to 'dance themselves free of it', and guild halls were refurbished with musicians provided to accommodate the dancing.

verdicts.claim: Modern medical historians attribute the dancing plague to mass psychogenic illness triggered by starvation and disease.
verdicts.note: Historian John Waller proposes the outbreak was a mass psychogenic illness/stress-induced psychosis triggered by extreme stress, starvation, and disease.

verdicts.claim: Mass psychogenic illness can cause uncontrollable muscle spasms and physical collapse during extreme psychological distress.
verdicts.note: The article links psychogenic movement disorder caused by psychological stress to chorea (unintentional movement/convulsions) and physical collapse.
